newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia sees high growth into next century.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia sees high growth into next century.

text.p: Indonesia should have per capita gross domestic product (GDP) of $3,800 by the year 2018, Coordinating Minister for Production and Distribution Hartarto said on Wednesday.

He told business leaders from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) and its trading partners that Indonesia would be among the world's five biggest economies by 2018, when its current 25-year development programme ends.
"GDP is projected to expand by just over six percent per year to in excess of eight percent towards the latter part of the plan period, producing an average annual growth of seven percent," he said.
"We are rather optimistic, because the first part we have already revised to over seven percent growth due to the performance in 1994, 1995 and 1996."
Hartarto said the government was also planning a decline in population growth to an annual rate of less than 0.9 percent by the end of the period.

"If we are able to reach seven percent growth and if we are able to reduce the population down to 0.7 percent (growth) by 2018, then Indonesia will have a GDP per capita of about $3,800 at 1993 constant prices with more equitable distribution," he said. "Indonesia will become one of the five biggest economies in the world with a nominal GDP of $2.0 trillion based on purchasing power parity."
He said the share of the industrial sector in the GDP would grow to 32.5 percent from the current 24 percent. "Then we can call Indonesia a new industrial country by 2018."
Hartarto reiterated previous forecasts that GDP growth in 1997 and 1998 was pegged at more than seven percent.
But he added that Indonesia needed to achieve a more equitable distribution of incomes, the eradication of poverty and the development of regions outside the islands of Java and Bali.

Hartarto said some 24 million Indonesians, out of a population of nearly 200 million, were living below the poverty line in 1994 and that the government had pledged to bring the number down to zero by 2008.

Some 600 business leaders from ASEAN -- which comprises Brunei, Indonesia, the Philippines, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- Europe, Asia and the United States are attending the two-day meeting.
